proposedchanges.description_short: At Least 16 Epstein Files Disappeared From DOJ Webpage, AP Reported

proposedchanges.title: PolitiFact Review Did Not Support Trump’s Claim He Kept All Promises
proposedchanges.description_short: PolitiFact Review Did Not Support Trump’s Claim He Kept All Promises
proposedchanges.description_medium: In January 2026, Trump told an audience in Detroit that he had “kept all my promises, and much more.” PBS NewsHour compared the statement with PolitiFact’s tracker of 75 second-term campaign promises. The review found some commitments completed and others stalled or incomplete, and concluded that the tracker did not support the absolute claim. It did not say every unfinished promise was abandoned.

evidencebasis: The latest long description identifies Trump’s Detroit statement, PolitiFact’s 75-promise tracker, and the review’s conclusion. It does not establish an oversight effect or systemic deception. The PBS URL remains in source_urls.
notes: The latest long description provides event detail and appropriate limits; the title and medium need to state that event directly.

proposedchanges.title: Trump Approved Federal Aid After Criticizing Local Leaders Over Potomac Spill
proposedchanges.description_short: Trump Approved Federal Aid After Criticizing Local Leaders Over Potomac Spill
proposedchanges.description_long:
A pipeline rupture on January 19 released at least 250 million gallons of sewage into the Potomac River. Washington, D.C., Mayor Muriel Bowser declared an emergency and requested federal assistance. Trump approved emergency resources, and FEMA said it could provide equipment and other support for the response. His approval followed public criticism of Bowser and Maryland Governor Wes Moore over the spill and its handling.

The aid addressed response needs after the rupture but did not resolve the dispute over responsibility for the damaged infrastructure or cleanup. The public statements describe the request, approval, and available federal support; they do not specify which resources were ultimately delivered or what environmental effects followed. The episode combined an emergency response involving federal and local officials with a political disagreement over responsibility. Approval of the request alone does not establish whether the aid was sufficient or when cleanup would be complete. Those questions remained separate from the decision to approve assistance.

evidencebasis: The packet and latest descriptions document the rupture, emergency declaration, aid request and approval, FEMA support, and public criticism of local leaders. The AP URL remains in source_urls.
notes: The medium and revised long distinguish the assistance decision from disputes over responsibility and later cleanup outcomes.

proposedchanges.title: Trump Criticized Maryland Governor Over Potomac Sewage Cleanup
proposedchanges.description_short: Trump Criticized Maryland Governor Over Potomac Sewage Cleanup
proposedchanges.description_long:
President Donald Trump blamed Maryland Governor Wes Moore for the Potomac River sewage spill, criticizing what he called a slow response to the January pipe rupture. The damaged pipe was under federal and District of Columbia water-authority jurisdiction. Trump said he would not allow local leadership to turn the river into a “Disaster Zone.”

Moore’s spokesman said EPA officials missed a recent state legislative hearing about cleanup and accused the administration of shirking its repair and cleanup responsibilities. Those were claims from the governor’s office; the report does not give a complete division of operational responsibility among the federal government, D.C. authorities, and Maryland. The exchange occurred while response to the sewage release continued. It brought a regional environmental emergency into a public dispute between the president and a state governor over jurisdiction, participation in a hearing, and remediation responsibility. The competing public statements did not resolve who was responsible for repair or cleanup.

evidencebasis: The packet and latest descriptions document Trump’s criticism, the reported jurisdiction, Moore’s office’s response, and the EPA hearing allegation. The AP URL remains in source_urls.
notes: The revised title and long preserve the competing claims without treating either as a final finding.

proposedchanges.description_medium: After a court dismissed Stormy Daniels’s defamation case in 2018, Donald Trump publicly called her “Horseface.” He celebrated the dismissal and directed the insult at her appearance rather than the legal arguments. CNBC reported that the remark was made on October 16, 2018, while the case was an active dispute between them. The comment did not change the court ruling.
proposedchanges.description_long: On October 16, 2018, Donald Trump responded to a court ruling dismissing Stormy Daniels’s defamation lawsuit by calling her “Horseface” and celebrating the dismissal. CNBC reported the remark and its connection to the litigation. Trump directed the insult at Daniels’s appearance rather than the legal issues in dispute. He was president at the time, and Daniels was a woman involved in a legal conflict with him. The comment paired his reaction to the court result with a personal, gendered insult. It placed a president’s public celebration of a ruling beside an appearance-based attack on a woman involved in litigation with him. The remark did not alter the ruling, and the report describes no further legal consequence arising from the comment. The event was a public response to an adverse court ruling, expressed through a personal insult rather than a legal argument about the case.

evidencebasis: The title identifies Trump’s insult and the court ruling. The medium and long describe the October 2018 remark, its link to the dismissed defamation suit, and the insult’s appearance-based nature without inventing legal consequences. The CNBC source URL is retained.
notes: Category, tags, and named people match the documented remark and litigation.
